title: Lesson 1: What is beta?
text: Beta tells you how much a stock moves compared with the whole market. A beta of 1 moves like the market. A beta of 2 tends to move twice as much, up and down. NVIDIA has a beta of about 2.2 and Rocket Lab about 2.6, so they are roller coasters. Eli Lilly is about 0.45, a much calmer ride.

title: Lesson 2: What is a price target?
text: A price target is an expert's guess of what a stock could be worth in about 12 months. The consensus is the average of many experts' guesses. GE trades near $309 and experts expect about $410, which is 33% higher. AMD is already at its target ($594 vs $608). Targets change often and are often wrong, so use them as a clue, not a promise.

title: Lesson 3: What is a dividend?
text: A dividend is a small payment that some companies send to their owners, usually every three months, just for holding the stock. Think of it as a thank-you share of the profits. Microsoft and Lockheed Martin pay dividends, while Amazon, AMD and Rocket Lab do not, because they keep their money to grow. The fund SCHD is built from companies that pay steady dividends, which is why it has been a calmer ride (beta 0.58). A dividend is not free money: the stock price usually drops a little when the dividend is paid.

title: Lesson 4: What is diversification?
text: Diversification means not putting all your eggs in one basket. On Monday, chip stocks fell (TSMC -2.0%, NVIDIA -1.3%) while Meta rose 3.4% and Microsoft rose 1.1%. If you owned only chip companies, you felt the whole drop. If you owned a mix, the ups and downs partly cancelled out. A fund like SPY holds about 500 companies at once, which is diversification in one purchase. It does not remove risk, and a mix can still go down when the whole market falls, but it can make the ride smoother.

title: Lesson 5: What is a P/E ratio?
text: P/E means price divided by earnings. Earnings are a company's profit for each share over the last year. If a stock costs $100 and the company earned $5 per share, the P/E is 20. You are paying $20 for every $1 of yearly profit. Today Alphabet's P/E is about 17, Microsoft's is about 30, and AMD's is about 154. A high P/E often means people expect fast growth, and a stock with a high P/E can fall harder if the growth is disappointing. A low P/E is not always a bargain either; sometimes the company is growing slowly. P/E works best when you compare similar companies.

title: Lesson 6: What is the 52 week range?
text: The 52 week range shows the lowest and highest price of a stock over the past year. It helps you see where today's price sits. AMD's range is $188.22 to $658.52, and it closed at $605.53, about 89% of the way up. Vertiv's range is $147.82 to $379.94, and it closed at $237.29, only about 39% of the way up. A price near the top means the stock has run a lot; a price near the bottom may mean people are worried, or that it is on sale. The range does not tell you which one is true. It only tells you where to start asking questions.

title: Lesson 7: What is dollar cost averaging?
text: Dollar cost averaging means putting in the same amount of money on a regular schedule, like $100 every month, no matter what the price is. Say a stock costs $10, then $8, then $12. Your $100 buys 10 shares, then 12.5, then 8.33, so you own 30.83 shares for $300. That is about $9.73 each, a little less than the $10 average price, because you automatically buy more when the price is low and fewer when it is high. Today is a good example: SPY fell 1.1%, and a person buying every month would simply get slightly more shares today than yesterday. It does not guarantee a profit and it does not protect from losses, but it takes away the stress of guessing the perfect day.

title: Lesson 8: Bonds vs stocks
text: A bond is a loan. You lend money to the government or a company, and they pay you interest and give the money back later. The 10 year US Treasury bond, a loan to the US government, paid an average of 4.99% in September, up from 4.06% a year earlier (see the chart on the board). When a very safe bond pays that much, stocks have to look attractive to compete, which is one reason expensive stocks wobble when yields rise. Stocks can grow more over many years but swing more; bonds usually swing less but grow less. Bonds are not risk free either: if rates rise, the price of an existing bond falls.

title: Lesson 9: ETFs vs single stocks
text: A single stock is a tiny piece of one company. An ETF (exchange traded fund) is a basket that holds pieces of many companies, and you buy the whole basket in one step. Look at today. NVIDIA, a single stock, fell 1.8%. The SPY fund, which holds 500 big US companies, rose 0.3%. The basket was calmer because the winners and losers in it partly cancel each other out. That is diversification, which Lesson 4 explained, built into one purchase. The tradeoff: a single stock can grow much faster than a basket if the company does great, but it can also fall much harder if the company stumbles. A basket will never be the top performer, and it will rarely be the worst. Many investors keep a basket as the base and add a few single stocks around it only if they understand each company.

title: Lesson 10: What is compound interest?
text: Compound interest means you earn growth on your growth. Say you invest $1,000 and it grows 7% in a year. You now have $1,070. Next year the 7% is applied to $1,070, not $1,000, so you gain $74.90 instead of $70. That small difference looks tiny at first, but it snowballs. At 7% a year, $1,000 becomes about $1,967 after 10 years and about $7,612 after 30 years. The most important ingredient is time, so starting early matters more than starting big. The 7% is only an example; real investments go up and down, and nothing is guaranteed.

title: Lesson 11: What is position sizing?
text: Position sizing means deciding how much money goes into each investment. Imagine you have $1,000 and put all of it in one stock that then drops 8% in a day, like Rocket Lab did today. You lose $80. If you had put only $100 in it, you would lose just $8. The riskier a stock swings, the smaller the slice many investors choose, so one bad day cannot hurt the whole plan. This is not advice to buy or sell anything; it is a way to think about how much any single idea matters to your total.

title: Lesson 12: What is market capitalization?
text: Market capitalization, or market cap, is the total price tag the stock market puts on a whole company. You get it by multiplying the share price by the number of shares. For example, Nvidia is worth about $5.2 trillion, while Rocket Lab is worth about $30 billion. A share price alone does not tell you which company is bigger: a $1,257 share of Eli Lilly and a $50 share of Rocket Lab come from companies of very different sizes. Bigger companies often swing less than small ones, but not always. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 13: What is an earnings report?
text: Four times a year, a public company must tell everyone how much it sold and how much it earned in the last three months. That report is called an earnings report. Analysts, who are people paid to study companies, make a guess ahead of time. If the real numbers beat the guess, the stock often jumps; if they fall short, it often drops, even when the company made a lot of money. What the company says about the next few months matters too. Lockheed Martin reports this Thursday, so it is a good one to watch. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 14: What is inflation?
text: Inflation means prices slowly rise over time, so the same dollar buys a little less each year. If a snack costs $1.00 today and prices rise 3% in a year, it costs $1.03 next year. Governments measure it with a report called the Consumer Price Index, or CPI. When inflation is higher than expected, the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates to cool things down, and that is why stock markets watch these reports so closely. It also shows why saving money in a place that earns nothing can lose buying power. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 15: What is a sector?
text: A sector is a group of companies that do a similar kind of work. Technology, healthcare, energy and banks are all sectors. Think of a school with different clubs: each club is a sector, and the students are the companies. Sectors often move in different directions on the same day. On Tuesday, healthcare stocks rose about 2% while energy and consumer staples fell. Holding companies from several sectors is one way to avoid putting all your eggs in one basket. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 16: What is volatility?
text: Volatility is how much a price jumps around. A calm stock moves a little each day, like a bike on a flat road. A volatile stock goes up and down a lot, like a bike on a hilly trail. You can see it in the 52 week range: AMD traded between about $188 and $659 in a year, while the Schwab dividend fund SCHD stayed between about $26 and $35. Volatility is not good or bad by itself. It just tells you how bumpy the ride might be, and it is why people who need their money soon often like calmer investments. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 17: Bull markets and bear markets
text: A bull market is a long stretch when prices mostly go up. A bear market is when they fall a lot, often 20% or more from a recent high. The names come from how the animals attack: a bull thrusts its horns up, a bear swipes down. In this board, the bear, base and bull numbers are three imagined futures, not predictions. Bear means a rough path, base means steady growth, and bull means a great path. Markets have always gone through both kinds of stretches, which is why patience matters. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 18: What is free cash flow?
text: Free cash flow is the money a company has left after paying its bills and its big spending on things like factories and computers. Think of a lemonade stand: sales minus lemons, cups and a new table is what you can really keep. A company with lots of free cash flow can pay dividends, buy back shares or save for hard times. A company that spends more than it earns for a while can still be fine if the spending builds something valuable, but it is something to watch. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 19: What is a pullback?
text: A pullback is when a stock or the whole market drops for a short time after rising. Think of climbing a hill: you sometimes stop and slide back a few steps before you keep going. Drops of 5% to 10% happen fairly often, even in healthy markets, and a drop of 20% or more is called a bear market. Today the Nasdaq 100 fund fell almost 3% in one day, which feels big, but it is a normal kind of event. A pullback is a good moment to ask what you own and why you own it, not to panic. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 20: What is a time horizon?
text: A time horizon is how long you plan to keep your money invested before you need it. Money for a bike next summer has a short horizon. Money for college in 10 years has a long one. This matters because stocks can fall a lot in a few weeks, like they did on Thursday, but over many years they have usually had time to recover. A short horizon means you cannot wait out a drop, so people usually keep that money in safer places like savings or bonds. A long horizon can handle more ups and downs. Before you look at any stock, ask yourself when you will need the money. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 21: What is the Federal Reserve?
text: The Federal Reserve, often called the Fed, is the central bank of the United States. One of its main jobs is to set a key interest rate that affects how much it costs to borrow money. When the Fed raises rates, loans like mortgages and car loans usually get more expensive, and bonds often pay more. When it lowers rates, borrowing gets cheaper. Stocks often react because company profits and investor moods change with the cost of money. The Fed meets several times a year and announces its decision, and investors watch every word. Next week the Fed meets again, which is why markets can feel jumpy beforehand. The Fed does not tell anyone what to buy or sell, and this is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 22: What is EPS (earnings per share)?
text: EPS stands for earnings per share. Take a company's profit for a period and divide it by the number of shares people own. If a company earns $100 and has 10 shares, EPS is $10. EPS lets us compare a big company and a small one on the same scale. During earnings season, news stories often say a company beat or missed what analysts expected for EPS. Beating the guess can lift a stock, and missing can drop it, even when the company is still making money. EPS is also the bottom part of the P/E ratio you learned in Lesson 5: price divided by EPS. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 23: What is a stock split?
text: A stock split is when a company cuts each share into smaller pieces. In a 2 for 1 split, if you own 1 share worth $100, you end up with 2 shares worth $50 each. Your total stays $100. It is like cutting a pizza into more slices: the pizza is the same size. Companies sometimes split so each share costs less and feels easier to buy. A split does not make a company worth more by itself. What matters is how well the business is doing. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 24: What is a profit margin?
text: A profit margin tells us how many cents a company keeps from each dollar it sells. Say a lemonade stand sells $100 of lemonade and, after paying for lemons, cups and helpers, keeps $20. Its profit margin is 20%. A higher margin means the company keeps more of each sale. NVIDIA keeps about 64 cents of each dollar, while Amazon keeps about 17 cents, because selling and shipping products costs a lot. A lower margin is not always bad, since it depends on the kind of business. Compare companies that do similar things. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 25: What is rebalancing?
text: Rebalancing means resetting your mix of investments back to the plan you chose. Say your plan is half in a stock fund and half in a bond fund. After stocks have a great year, the stock part might grow to 70% of your money. That is riskier than you planned. Rebalancing means moving some money back toward 50/50. It keeps your risk close to what you meant it to be. Some people rebalance once a year, or when the mix drifts a lot. It can feel odd to trim what is winning, but the goal is steady risk, not chasing the best performer. This is for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.

title: Lesson 26: What is an expense ratio?
text: An expense ratio is the yearly fee a fund charges, shown as a percent of your money. If a fund charges 0.10% and you hold $1,000, you pay about $1 a year. It comes out of the fund automatically, so you never get a bill. Funds like SPY, QQQ and SCHD usually charge low fees, while some funds charge much more. Small fees add up over many years, because that money can no longer grow for you. When you compare two similar funds, the fee is one easy thing to check.

title: Lesson 27: What is revenue?
text: Revenue is all the money a company brings in from selling things, before it pays any bills. Profit is what is left after paying for workers, parts, and taxes. Imagine a lemonade stand that sells $100 of lemonade but spends $70 on lemons, cups, and sugar. Revenue is $100, and profit is $30. Investors watch revenue growth because a company that sells more each year may keep growing. When Vertiv says its sales rose 61%, that is revenue growth. But growing sales do not always mean growing profit, so it helps to check both.

title: Lesson 28: What is guidance?
text: Guidance is a company's own forecast of its sales or profit for the next few months. Think of a student who says, 'I expect to get a B on the next test.' If the student gets an A, people are happy. If it is a C, people are let down. Investors pay close attention to guidance because stocks are about the future. Microsoft's forecast this week said it expects its sales to grow 18% to 19% next quarter. A company can have a great past quarter and still see its stock fall if its guidance sounds weak. Remember that a forecast is a guess, not a promise.

title: Lesson 29: What is capex?
text: Capex is short for capital expenditure. It is the money a company spends on big things it will use for years, like buildings, machines and computer chips. Think of a pizza shop that buys a new oven. The oven costs a lot today, but it can make pizzas for years. Right now, giant tech companies are spending tens of billions of dollars on data centers for AI. That can help them grow later, but it also leaves less cash in the bank today. This week, Alphabet's capex was bigger than the cash its business brought in, and investors did not like that. When you read about a company, check both how much it spends and what it earns from that spending.

title: Lesson 30: What is a market index?
text: A market index is a list of companies used as a scoreboard for the market. The S&P 500 follows 500 large US companies. The Nasdaq 100 follows 100 big companies listed on the Nasdaq, many of them tech. Think of it like a class average: it tells you how the group is doing, not how any one student did. Funds like SPY and QQQ copy these lists, so buying one fund gives you a small piece of every company inside. When you hear that the market fell 1%, people usually mean an index like the S&P 500 fell 1%. Some stocks in the index may still have gone up that day, like Eli Lilly on Thursday.

title: Lesson 31: What is a market correction?
text: A correction is when a stock or an index falls at least 10% from its recent high. It is a normal part of investing and happens often, usually every year or two. A drop of 20% or more is called a bear market. The Nasdaq is now about 7.8% below its October high, so it is close to correction territory. Corrections can feel scary, but they are also the price investors pay for growth over many years. A long time horizon, a mix of different investments, and not selling in a panic are the usual tools people use to stay calm.

title: Lesson 32: What is the 10 year Treasury yield?
text: When the US government borrows money, it sells bonds called Treasuries. The 10 year Treasury yield is the yearly interest the government pays on a bond that lasts 10 years. People watch it because it works like a base price for money. When the yield goes up, safe bonds look more attractive, and investors may pay less for stocks, especially fast-growing tech companies whose profits come far in the future. On our board, the monthly average yield rose from about 4.3% in April to 4.99% in September. A rising yield does not mean stocks must fall, but it is one reason prices can swing.

title: Lesson 33: What is concentration risk?
text: Concentration risk means having too much of your money tied to one company, one industry or one idea. If that one thing has a bad day, your whole pile feels it. Today is a good example. Chip makers like AMD, Vertiv and TSMC often move together, so owning only chip stocks can feel like owning one big bet. Spreading money across different kinds of companies, such as health care, defense or broad index funds, can soften a rough day in one area. It does not remove risk, and it does not guarantee gains. It just helps one surprise matter less.

title: Lesson 34: Market orders and limit orders
text: When you buy a stock, you choose how to place the order. A market order says, buy now at whatever price is available. It is fast, but the price can be a little different from the one you saw, especially in the first minutes after the market opens when prices jump around. A limit order says, buy only at this price or better. You set the price, but the order may never happen if the stock does not reach it. Neither one is better for everyone. Many people who are learning like limit orders because they teach patience and show exactly what you agreed to pay. This is education, not advice.

title: Lesson 35: What is after-hours trading?
text: The regular stock market opens at 9:30 in the morning and closes at 4:00 in the afternoon, New York time. But some trading also happens before the open and after the close. That is called extended hours or after-hours trading. Companies often share their results right after the close, so prices can move fast in the evening. There are fewer buyers and sellers then, so prices can jump around more and be harder to get at a fair price. That is why many learners wait for the next regular open before reacting to news. This is education, not advice.

title: Lesson 36: What is trading volume?
text: Volume is the number of shares that change hands in a day. Think of a school cafeteria: a busy lunch line means many people are buying, and an empty one means few. On Tuesday about 90 million NVIDIA shares traded, while the usual day is closer to 120 million. High volume on a big price move suggests many people agree with the move. A big move on very low volume can be less reliable, because only a few trades pushed the price. Volume is a clue, not a promise. This is education, not advice.

title: Lesson 37: Why can a stock fall on good news?
text: A stock price is not only about how a company did. It is also about what people expected. Imagine you hoped for an A on a test and got a B plus. The grade is good, but you feel let down. Investors feel the same way. If a company reports strong results but investors hoped for even more, the price can drop. The reverse can happen too: a company with weak results can rise if people feared something worse. This is why smart investors ask two questions: how did the company do, and how did that compare with what everyone expected?

title: Lesson 38: What is dividend yield?
text: Dividend yield tells you how much a company pays in dividends each year compared with its stock price. If a stock costs $100 and pays $2 a year, the yield is 2%. Today TSMC's yield is about 1.1%, Microsoft's is about 0.65%, and NVIDIA's is about 0.26%, so they pay little. SCHD, the fund built from steady dividend payers, holds companies that pay more. Here is the catch: the yield changes when the price changes. If a stock falls and the dividend stays the same, the yield goes up, but that is not a gift, because you just lost value in the price. A high yield can also be a warning sign that people doubt the company can keep paying. Yield is one clue, never the whole story.

title: Lesson 39: What is panic selling?
text: Panic selling is when people rush to sell because prices are falling and they are scared, not because they have a plan. Here is the problem. If you sell after a big drop, you turn a temporary paper loss into a real one. Also, nobody can predict the exact bottom. Look at history: stocks have fallen sharply many times, like in April 2025, and then later recovered, though that is never guaranteed. Before investing, ask yourself two things. How long can I leave this money alone? How would I feel if it fell 20% in a week? If the honest answer is 'I would hate it', that is useful to know, and a mix of steadier investments might fit better. Planning for bad days in advance is much easier than deciding during one.

title: Lesson 40: What is the jobs report?
text: Once a month, the US government counts how many people got new jobs. That count is the jobs report. It also shows the unemployment rate, which is the share of people who want a job but do not have one. Why does a stock market care? A strong report means the economy is running hot, which can push the Fed to keep interest rates high. A weak report can worry people about companies earning less. Sometimes good news for workers makes stocks fall, because investors fear higher rates. The takeaway: the market often reacts to what the report means for interest rates, not only to the number itself.

title: Lesson 41: What is a relief rally?
text: A relief rally is a quick jump in prices after a big fall, when people feel a little less scared. Today is a good example. After a very rough day yesterday, many stocks bounced, and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ rose 1.4%. Here is the catch. A bounce is not the same as a recovery. A stock that falls 20% needs to rise 25% just to get back to where it started. Sometimes prices keep falling after a bounce, and sometimes they keep rising. Nobody knows in advance. That is why many investors stick to a plan made on calm days instead of reacting to each big up or down day.

title: Lesson 42: Growth stocks and value stocks
text: People often sort stocks into two groups. A growth stock is a company expected to grow fast, so investors pay a high price for it today. They hope the business keeps getting bigger. A value stock looks cheap compared with what the company earns, and it often pays a dividend. Look at our list. AMD has a P/E of about 96, which means investors pay $96 for each $1 of yearly profit. That is a bet on fast growth. Alphabet has a P/E of about 15, which looks more like a value price. Growth stocks can rise a lot, but they usually swing more and can fall harder when interest rates are high. Neither type is better. Many investors own a mix.

title: Lesson 43: What is correlation?
text: Correlation means how much two things move together. Today is a good example. Almost every stock on our list went up at the same time, because the whole market felt better. When stocks move together, we say they are highly correlated. This matters for safety. If you own five stocks that all rise and fall together, you are not really spread out. Owning different kinds of things, like a dividend fund, a health company and a tech company, can help because they do not always move the same way. Notice that NVIDIA fell today while its rivals rose. Stocks can also go their own way when there is news about one company.

title: Lesson 44: What is an earnings report?
text: Four times a year, public companies share a report card called an earnings report. It tells us how much they sold, how much profit they made, and what they expect next. Investors do not only look at whether the numbers were good. They compare them to what experts guessed beforehand. A company can make record profits and still see its stock drop if people hoped for even more. That is why prices can jump or fall fast on earnings day. NVIDIA's report on November 17 is a good example to follow along with.

title: Lesson 45: What is key person risk?
text: Some companies depend a lot on one leader, often the founder or CEO. Key person risk is the chance that something happening to that one person hurts the whole company. It could be health, a scandal, or the person leaving. When investors worry about a leader, the stock can fall even if the company's products and sales have not changed at all. That is what we saw with NVIDIA this week. Good companies try to lower this risk by building a strong team and a clear plan for who would take over. It is one more reason why owning many companies, not just one, can help.

title: Lesson 46: What is a rate hike?
text: The Federal Reserve sets a key interest rate. That rate affects how much it costs to borrow money for things like houses, cars and business loans. A rate hike means the Fed raises that rate. The Fed usually does this to slow down rising prices, called inflation. When borrowing costs more, people and companies tend to spend less, and prices cool off. Stocks often fall when a hike looks more likely, because companies may earn less and safe savings accounts and bonds start to pay more. That is why yesterday's hot inflation report pushed stocks down.

title: Lesson 47: What is an analyst downgrade?
text: Analysts are people at banks and research firms who study companies all day. They give each stock a rating, like Buy, Neutral or Sell, and a price target, which is their guess of where the price could be in about a year. A downgrade means an analyst lowers that rating, for example from Buy to Neutral. Today Baird did this with NVIDIA. A downgrade can push a price down for a day, but it is one opinion, not a fact. Different analysts often disagree, and they can be wrong. It is smarter to look at many opinions and at the company's real results than to react to one headline.
